Early images are mostly close to the arched harp, and players already appear on Gupta-period coins and in cave reliefs. From about the sixth century, images of the goddess Saraswati mostly show a zither-like veena, which later split into the North Indian rudra veena and the South Indian Saraswati veena; the first has largely been replaced by the sitar today, while the second is still used in Carnatic classical music.

The North Indian rudra veena has two large gourd resonators, while the South Indian Saraswati veena replaces the lower gourd with a pear-shaped wooden body; both have four melody strings, three drone strings and twenty-four frets, and can play three octaves. The right hand plucks the melody strings with a plectrum and sweeps the drone strings with the little finger, while the left hand stops the frets and can damp the sympathetic strings, which is how the sustain and the timbre are controlled. The long, hollow neck makes slides and legato easy; the fretless veena uses a glass slide and sounds close to a humming voice.

The traditional body is made of a special wood, hollowed out; the North Indian rudra veena has large gourd resonators at both ends, and the South Indian Saraswati veena replaces the lower gourd with a pear-shaped wooden body. Modern designs may use fibreglass or other materials instead of hollowed wood and gourds. The strings include metal ones, seven in all for melody and drone; the plectrum is made of metal wire, and the fretless veena is stopped with an egg-shaped or round glass slide. The materials of the other parts are not recorded.

The veena (Veena) is a class of plucked instruments of the Indian subcontinent, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 312.322. The common forms divide into fretted and fretless: the North Indian rudra veena is used in Hindustani classical music and is a stick zither, about 1 to 1.2 metres long, with a large resonating gourd at each end; the South Indian Saraswati veena is used in Carnatic classical music and is a long-necked pear-shaped lute with 24 frets. Both usually have four melody strings and three drone strings, and are laid across the lap to play, the right hand plucking the melody strings with a finger or plectrum and the little finger the drone strings, while the left hand stops or damps the strings.
